title: LabWired allows engineers to test compiled firmware on simulated MCU boards (CPU and peripherals)
summary: Andrii Shylenko s LabWired is an MIT-licensed MCU firmware simulation core that runs compiled firmware against modeled CPUs and peripherals, captures UART and bus output, register state, and supports repeatable checks in CI. The simulator works on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M3, Cortex-M4, Cortex-M7, Cortex-M33 cores, RISC-V architecutre, and Xtensa LX6 and LX7 (some ESP32 parts). The main benefit of the project is speeding up firmware testing since doing some on real boards is slow. The hardware must be ready, then the firmware must be flashed to the board each time you want to test it, and if something breaks, developers get a dark LED and no trace. If a firmware project needs to support multiple boards, this quickly adds up. The project is different from a CPU/MCU emulator for two main reasons: The full board is modeled, not only the chip. Sensors, displays, and bus devices are also simulated. title: ControlBox Home Assistant solution is designed for floor heating systems, house lighting, 1-wire sensors (Crowdfunding)
summary: DomeCtrl s ControlBox is a Raspberry Pi 5-based controller running Home Assistant and primarily designed for hydronic radiant floor heating (RFH) systems. It also supports lighting solutions and integration with energy devices such as solar collectors, photovoltaic installations, heat pumps, hydraulic pumps & valves. The system controls thermal valves, hydraulic PWM pumps, and related RFH devices, and can read multiple 1-wire temperature sensors over long cables (>6 m). The ControlBox also features 32 LED-strip output channels, for up to 2 kW output. title: 280 MHz STMicro STM32G5 Cortex-M33 mixed-signal MCU targets digital power and motor control applications
summary: The STM32G5 series is a family of 280 MHz Arm Cortex-M33 mixed-signal MCUs designed for industrial power supplies, photovoltaic inverters, EV chargers, robotics, and motor control systems. It doubles the performance of the older STM32G4 series unveiled in 2021. The new MCU family features up to 512KB flash, 112KB SRAM with ECC, a 111 ps high-resolution timer (HRTIM) with up to 12 PWM outputs on some variants, and 12-bit ADCs supporting up to 5 MSPS. Other features include position encoder interfaces, a 16-element programmable logic array, CORDIC and FMAC mathematical accelerators, and security features such as Arm TrustZone, secure boot, and post-quantum cryptography support.
